parts.title: Booking a ferry crossing
parts.context: A man books a ferry crossing for his family and dog.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a ferry company to book a crossing for his family. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Channel Crossings, Ingrid speaking.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Good morning. I'd like to book a ferry crossing for my family, please, from Dover to Calais.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Of course. I'll need a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The crossing is to Calais, so 'Calais' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Could I have your surname, please?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: It's Garrett. That's G-A-R-R-E-T-T.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Thank you, Mr Garrett. And which date would you like to travel?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: The fourteenth of August.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: And how many people will be travelling?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Two adults and three children. We have a big family.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Are you taking a vehicle?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Yes, our car, and we're bringing our dog as well. Is that allowed?

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Yes, but pets must travel in the kennels on the car deck, and I'll need to note that on the booking. What time would you like to leave?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Eight in the morning, if you have space. Half past seven would be better, but I imagine that's full.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: It is, I'm afraid. The eight o'clock is fine, though.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: The fare is forty-five pounds for each adult, and the car is charged separately.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: What about the children?

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: Children under five travel free, and from five to fifteen they pay half. How old are yours?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Four, seven and ten. So only one is free, I suppose.

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: That's right. Now, about your dog. The kennels are on the car deck, and you can visit him during the crossing, but only with a member of the crew.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That's good to know. He's quite nervous. Can we upgrade to a more comfortable seat?

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: There are reclining seats for an extra ten pounds each. They're popular with families who have an early crossing, because the children can sleep.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That sounds worth it. When do we need to arrive at the port?

script.speaker: ingrid
script.text: You must check in at least ninety minutes before departure, as there are passport checks and the car has to be inspected.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Thank you. I'll book it now.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A co-working space
parts.context: A manager shows prospective members round a co-working space.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a manager showing prospective members round a co-working space. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Hive. I'm Elena Ferrari, the community manager. Please look at the plan. We're at reception, near the entrance at the bottom, and the open-plan area, where most members work, is in the middle.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: Along the top, in the middle, are the meeting rooms. There are four of them, and members can book them online by the hour. At the top on the right is the quiet room, where phones and conversations aren't allowed.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: At the top on the left is the terrace, which has tables and plants, and it's very popular in summer. On the left side, in the middle, is the kitchen, with free tea and coffee. And on the right side, in the middle, is the printing area, with a printer, a scanner and a stock of paper.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: Below those are the phone booths, at the bottom on the left, and the storage lockers, at the bottom on the right.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: Some more information. We have eighty desks, and most of them are rented by freelancers and small companies. At the moment about seventy are occupied, so there is room for you.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: Members have access to the building twenty-four hours a day, with a key card, which is useful if you work with clients in other time zones.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: The monthly fee includes tea and coffee, wifi and the use of the meeting rooms for ten hours a month. Printing is charged separately, at a few pence a page.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: On Friday afternoons, we hold a networking event, with drinks and snacks, which is free and open to all members. It's a good way to meet people from other businesses.

script.speaker: ferrari
script.text: If you'd like to try us before you commit, you can book a free day pass online. Just choose a date on our website, and we'll have a desk waiting for you. Now, if you'd like to follow me, I'll show you the terrace.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A soil survey on a farm
parts.context: Two students write up the results of a soil survey.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two agriculture students, Maeve and Luis, writing up a soil survey of a farm. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: Luis, we need to decide how to describe our sampling method. We took samples from five fields on the farm.

script.speaker: luis
script.text: Fifteen from each field, I think, walking in a W pattern across it, so that we'd cover the whole area.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: That's right. And we took them with a hand auger, to a depth of twenty centimetres.

script.speaker: luis
script.text: Yes, because that's the layer where most of the plant roots grow. Then we mixed the samples from each field together.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: Mr Hale asked us not to take samples near the hedges. Do you remember why?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: Because the soil there isn't typical. Leaves fall from the hedge and rot, so it contains much more organic matter than the rest of the field.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: The analysis was done by a commercial laboratory, wasn't it?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: Yes, the university lab was fully booked, so Dr Green arranged for a laboratory in town to do it. The results came back on Tuesday.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: And what's our main recommendation to Mr Hale?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: To add lime to the most acidic field. That would have the biggest effect on his crop yields, and it's cheap and easy to do.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: Now let's go through the results field by field. North Field first.

script.speaker: luis
script.text: It's low in organic matter. The farmer has grown wheat there for many years without adding any manure.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: River Field?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: It was waterlogged. We found standing water just below the surface, and the drainage is poor.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: Hill Field?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: That's very compacted, because the heavy machinery goes over it every year, so the water can't soak in.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: The Orchard?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: That was the best. The soil was rich in worms, and we counted more than twenty in every spade of earth.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: And the Meadow?

script.speaker: luis
script.text: That was too acidic, which is why the grass is so poor there. That's the field that needs lime.

script.speaker: maeve
script.text: Good. Let's put that in a table, and write the recommendations next.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the origins of the Olympic Games
parts.context: A lecture on the ancient Games and their revival.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the origins of the Olympic Games. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we'll look at the origins of the Olympic Games, and how they developed from a local festival into the world's biggest sporting event.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, in southern Greece, and the first recorded Games were in seven hundred and seventy-six BC. They took place every four years for nearly twelve hundred years. They were a religious festival, in honour of the god Zeus, and the great temple there held a huge statue of him.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One striking feature was the sacred truce. While the Games were on, wars were suspended, so that athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia, even across territories at war.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The events included running, wrestling, boxing and chariot racing. The shortest race, the stadion, was about two hundred metres, and the first Games had no other event. The winners received no money, only a wreath of olive leaves, though they were treated as heroes when they returned home.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Competition was limited. Only free Greek men could compete, and women, slaves and foreigners were excluded. The Games survived under Roman rule, but at the end of the fourth century, a Christian emperor banned them as a pagan festival.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Games were revived in the late nineteenth century, thanks to a Frenchman, Baron Pierre de Coubertin. The first modern Games were held in Athens in eighteen ninety-six, with fourteen nations taking part.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Women first competed in nineteen hundred, in sports such as tennis and golf, and the first Winter Games were held in nineteen twenty-four, with sports like skiing and skating. And the tradition of the Olympic flame continues today. It is lit at Olympia, using a mirror and the rays of the sun, and then carried by torch to the host city. Next week we'll look at the Paralympic Games.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
